sources.citation: Tournadre, Nicolas & Hiroyuki Suzuki. 2023. The Tibetic Languages: An introduction to the family of languages derived from Old Tibetan. Villejuif: LACITO-Publications. 1151 pp.
sources.note: Nothing for Laya. Ch. 9.7.2 p. 555 says Laya, Lingzhi and Lunana are three yakherd varieties of Dzongkha that 'have so far not been studied'; p. 557 and App. 3 p. 1033 only locate Laya (Dzongkha dialect 72.1, map I7). The book's stress discussion (sec. 7.3.3-7.3.4, pp. 241-243) concerns Lhasa/Amdo etc. Grep of the full text for 'Laya' (excluding 'Himalaya') yields only these three passages.

sources.citation: Tshering, Karma & George van Driem. 2019. The Grammar of Dzongkha: Revised and Expanded. Santa Barbara: Himalayan Linguistics. (revision of van Driem & Tshering 1998, Dzongkha, Languages of the Greater Himalayan Region 1)
sources.note: Nothing for Laya. Ch. 1 p. 4: 'Peculiar dialects of Dzongkha are spoken in the far north, viz. the dialect of the alpine yakherd communities of 'Lingzhi, Laya and Lunana... Much of the couleur locale of these northern dialects results from structural and lexical similarities with Tibetan.' The phonology is explicitly 'based on a single prestige variety' (Wang/Thê); no other Laya mentions apart from example sentences and a place-name list.

sources.citation: Watters, Stephen A. 2018. A grammar of Dzongkha (dzo): phonology, words, and simple clauses. PhD dissertation, Rice University.
sources.note: Nothing for Laya: 'Layakha' occurs only in the gloss of a text example (p. 165, ex. 42a, a speaker saying Layakha words cannot be understood). Stress statements there are about standard Dzongkha.
